purpose: Thiamine, also known as Vitamin B1, is used to prevent or treat a thiamine deficiency in your body. It is important for helping your body turn food into energy. Doctors may also prescribe it for conditions caused by low thiamine levels, such as Wernicke's encephalopathy, which affects the brain and nervous system.
how_it_works: Your body cannot make thiamine on its own, so you need to get it from food or supplements. Thiamine helps your cells produce energy by breaking down carbohydrates from the food you eat. It also plays a key role in keeping your nerves and heart working properly.
common_side_effects: Thiamine is generally very well tolerated. Some people may notice mild upset stomach, nausea, or a warm or flushed feeling, especially with injections. A slight skin rash or itching can occasionally occur.
warnings: Rarely, some people can have a serious allergic reaction, especially with the injectable form — signs include trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a rapid heartbeat. Tell your doctor if you have any allergies before receiving thiamine injections. If you drink alcohol heavily, your doctor needs to know, as alcohol greatly reduces how well your body absorbs thiamine.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on why you are taking it. For a simple dietary supplement, a typical adult dose is 1 to 2 mg per day taken by mouth. For treating a deficiency or serious conditions, doses can be much higher — sometimes 50 to 100 mg or more per day, given by mouth or by injection. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your situation.
